subjects.displayTitle: Teaching the Cause: the call to every believer
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh lays the duty of teaching His Cause on every soul who recognizes Him and calls it the most meritorious of all deeds; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá goes further and names it the greatest of God’s gifts, the corner-stone on which everything else is built. A duty that is also a gift asks for something other than eloquence. The sword has been set aside and victory is to come through utterance, yet the word that reaches another heart is spoken by a life: character before argument, friendship before proof, a heart detached enough that its speech carries fire rather than self. To guide one soul, the Báb says, is better than possessing all that is on earth, for lamp is lit from lamp and one holy soul becomes the cause of life to a hundred thousand. The road runs inward first, to teaching oneself before others and to the prayer that makes a teacher a channel for the Holy Spirit, and then outward, to the confirmations promised to whoever arises and to the quiet power of a single soul.

Bahá’u’lláh writes, Teach ye the Cause of God, O people of Bahá, for God hath prescribed unto every one the duty of proclaiming His Message, and regardeth it as the most meritorious of all deeds. Elsewhere He says the obligation has been imposed upon every one, and bids His loved ones repose not on their couches but unloose their tongues. In His Will and Testament ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls teaching the greatest of all the gifts of God and our first obligation, the head corner-stone of the foundation itself. His Tablets ask each friend to teach at least one soul within a year, and tell one who could not decide between writing and teaching that for the present teaching is preferable. The call also reaches those who feel unready: Bahá’u’lláh says that one who is not eloquent may assist the teacher, and one prevented by worldly obstacles may appoint a deputy. Why do the Writings make teaching the duty of every believer rather than of a few? What do the provisions for those unable to speak suggest about what the duty asks?
shortened: Say: Teach ye the Cause of God, O people of Bahá, for God hath prescribed unto every one the duty of proclaiming His Message, and regardeth it as the most meritorious of all deeds. Such a deed is acceptable only when he that teacheth the Cause is already a firm believer in God, the Supreme Protector, the Gracious, the Almighty. He hath, moreover, ordained that His Cause be taught through the power of men’s utterance, and not through resort to violence.

shortened: In these days, the most important of all things is the guidance of the nations and peoples of the world. Teaching the Cause is of utmost importance for it is the head corner-stone of the foundation itself.

Bahá’u’lláh calls the command to teach the greatest and most mighty after the recognition of God, citing the verse that whoso quickens a soul is as though he had quickened all humanity, and He calls His loved ones the world’s spiritual physicians. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names the station of a teacher the greatest of all stations, and compares the herald of the Kingdom to a farmer whose station is raised in the estimation of the lord of the village. Images of increase recur: the lamp from which lamp after lamp is lit, the one who plants trees that others may benefit, the chain through which one holy soul becomes the cause of life to a hundred thousand. Reported talks speak of the joy that teaching brings. Why is the guidance of a single soul weighed against all the riches of the earth? What does the image of the chain add to it?
shortened: Today, there is no result or fruit greater than guiding the people, because these helpless creatures, especially the Persians, have remained without a share in the bestowals of God.

These readings turn to the instruments of teaching. Bahá’u’lláh says that to assist Him is to teach His Cause, and that although He could render the Cause victorious through a single word, He has ordained that complete victory be achieved through speech and utterance; the decree of holy war by the sword has been lifted. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls utterance the world-conquering sword of the friends, a sword that taketh not life but bestoweth it. Wisdom governs its use. Bahá’u’lláh asks that one speak to each soul according to its capacity, that the earth first be made receptive and then the word delivered, and He says that one who cries out for people to rend their veils is not counted among the teachers; wisdom, He explains, means such deeds as cause the heedless to become aware. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that wisdom is steadfastness in teaching, not silence and fear, and counsels gentle speech and argument in the most excellent manner. A reported talk warns against thrusting the teachings on unwilling listeners. How can wisdom restrain speech without becoming an excuse for silence? What makes a word attract rather than repel?
shortened: It behoveth the people of Baha to render the Lord victorious through the power of their utterance and to admonish the people by their goodly deeds and character, inasmuch as deeds exert greater influence than words.

Say: If it be Our pleasure We shall render the Cause victorious through the power of a single word from Our presence.

However, since Our loving providence surpasseth all things, We have ordained that complete victory should be achieved through speech and utterance, that Our servants throughout the earth may thereby become the recipients of divine good. This is but a token of God's bounty vouchsafed unto them.

These readings look inward, at the one who teaches. Bahá’u’lláh says that unless the heart is detached words have no effect, and that when the teacher is enkindled with the fire of His love and adorned with detachment, his words will set ablaze those that hear him. He asks His servants to speak for the sake of God and to look not to rejection or acceptance but to the service they have been bidden. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that we must first remember ourselves and then turn to others, for one who has not found existence cannot bestow it, and that one who has taught himself will be able to teach others. He describes travellers who went seeking fame and fortune and returned utterly disappointed, and a reported talk says confirmations do not accompany those who would gather a group around themselves. Teaching is called a gift of God, not a matter of talent or learning, and Bahá’u’lláh tells one who lacked outward learning not to grieve. The Báb asks that one journey only if no sorrow is found in the heart. What does detachment mean for a teacher in practice? Why would motive change the effect of the same words?
shortened: Speak ye for the sake of God and teach His Cause for His sake. Look not to rejection or acceptance, but rather to the service whereunto ye have been bidden by God. This is the most great favor, eternal success, everlasting fruit, and the bestowal of Truth at all times, and His outpouring grace hath reached and shall continue to reach in every season.

He asks His servants to speak for the sake of God and to look not to rejection or acceptance but to the service they have been bidden. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that we must first remember ourselves and then turn to others, for one who has not found existence cannot bestow it, and that one who has taught himself will be able to teach others. He describes travellers who went seeking fame and fortune and returned utterly disappointed, and a reported talk says confirmations do not accompany those who would gather a group around themselves. Teaching is called a gift of God, not a matter of talent or learning, and Bahá’u’lláh tells one who lacked outward learning not to grieve. The Báb asks that one journey only if no sorrow is found in the heart. What does detachment mean for a teacher in practice? Why would motive change the effect of the same words?
shortened: To teach is a gift of God and is not based on one's talents. To present proofs and convincing evidence is but a bounty from the All Merciful and is not dependent on knowledge and learning. How often has one unlettered soul become the source of guidance for the entire world.

order.why: These readings concern the one who hears. Bahá’u’lláh says that if one is found who thirsts he should be given the pure wine, and otherwise it should be preserved in its vessel; if one is receptive, cast upon him the melodies of the Spirit, and if he turns away, turn unto God. Whenever the fire of search appears in a soul, mention the Desired One to him, and consort with all religions with joy and fragrance. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá compares the teacher to a wise farmer who scatters seed in rich soil, and asks that the Word be conveyed according to capacity, with feasts of fellowship that attract hearts. He suggests approaches for different hearers: prominent people who will lead others troop after troop, the gatherings of the Theosophical Society, and an official coming little by little to believe. Reported talks advise speaking to the irreligious of what distinguishes humans from the animal kingdom, and recall the seed that fell by the wayside. Should response lessen, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes, be not saddened, for we are commanded to sow and the growth rests with God. How can a teacher discern readiness without judging others? What does the farmer’s patience teach?

These readings gather accounts of those who taught. A recorded account gives the Báb’s words bidding a follower to be engaged in a mosque in prayer and in teaching. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells of a believer led about the streets with a halter who, composed and smiling, kept on speaking to the people, and of another who, bound in chains, never wavered in teaching. He recalls Paul, who after severe beatings arose and proclaimed the Cause in the nearby city, and Bahá’u’lláh recalls that Peter was a fisher of fish and Abu Dharr a shepherd. Reported talks tell of an illiterate man in Persia who guided many great men through his pure love of God, a village woman who in one year lit forty lamps, and a man who resolved to hunt souls rather than animals. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá also describes His own journeys: in a reported talk He recalls that, weary in America, He would first concentrate on the Blessed Beauty and then His voice would be raised, and a Tablet recalls His going to Montreal though warned against it. What do these lives have in common? Which example speaks most directly to your own circumstances?

The guide closes with prayers for teaching. Bahá’u’lláh trusts that God will aid Him and His servants to exalt His name, to deliver His Message and to proclaim His Cause, and asks to be assisted so to teach that the dead may speed out of their sepulchers and rush forth towards God. In another prayer He says that, though the lover be loth to share with any one the intimate conversation of his beloved, whenever the commandment to declare the Cause reaches Him He will unhesitatingly obey it, undeterred by the darts of affliction. Other prayers ask to arise with bared head and cry out God’s name amidst His creatures, and recall arising, when His summons came, to call all in heaven and earth to His favors. A prayer of the Báb in a recorded account asks that the infant seed of God may soon germinate in the hearts of men and grow into a mighty tree beneath whose shadow all peoples may gather. How do these prayers join the inner life of devotion to the outward work of teaching? Which of their requests could become a daily prayer?

In another prayer He says that, though the lover be loth to share with any one the intimate conversation of his beloved, whenever the commandment to declare the Cause reaches Him He will unhesitatingly obey it, undeterred by the darts of affliction. Other prayers ask to arise with bared head and cry out God’s name amidst His creatures, and recall arising, when His summons came, to call all in heaven and earth to His favors. A prayer of the Báb in a recorded account asks that the infant seed of God may soon germinate in the hearts of men and grow into a mighty tree beneath whose shadow all peoples may gather. How do these prayers join the inner life of devotion to the outward work of teaching? Which of their requests could become a daily prayer?
shortened: Do Thou destine for me, O my God, what becometh the greatness of Thy majesty, and assist me, by Thy strengthening grace, so to teach Thy Cause that the dead may speed out of their sepulchers, and rush forth towards Thee, trusting wholly in Thee, and fixing their gaze upon the orient of Thy Cause, and the dawning-place of Thy Revelation.

I would proclaim Thee, undeterred by the darts of affliction that may rain down upon me from the clouds of Thy decree.
I swear by Thy might! Neither the hosts of the earth nor those of heaven can keep me back from revealing the things I am commanded to manifest.

In these authorized words from a talk in Paris, reported in Paris Talks, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks His hearers to live and act in direct obedience to the teachings and laws of Bahá’u’lláh, so that everyone may see that in word and in deed they are His followers, and to exert themselves so that this glorious teaching may encircle the globe. The supplied quotation differs only in spelling; the approximate status is preserved. Read it with the readings on deeds and character. Why does He place living the teachings before spreading them?

This supplied counsel, written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi in 1953, says that success in teaching needs complete dedication, consecration to spreading the Faith and the living of the Bahá’í life, because that creates the magnet for the Holy Spirit, and the individual should be as a reed through which the Spirit flows to give new life to the seeking soul. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Compare it with the readings on the teacher’s heart. What does the image of the reed ask of the teacher?

This supplied passage from the Ridván 1998 message of the Universal House of Justice says that the individual is charged by Bahá’u’lláh Himself with teaching, the most meritorious of all deeds, and is directly responsible to Him for it; it quotes Shoghi Effendi’s advice not to wait for directions or special encouragement, nor be deterred by obstacles or critics. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Read it with the readings on the call to every believer. What does direct responsibility to Bahá’u’lláh change?
shortened: But beyond the necessity of responding to the call of the institutions, the individual is charged by Baha'u'llah Himself with the sacred duty of teaching His Cause, described by Him as the "most meritorious of all deeds." So long as there are souls in need of enlightenment, this duty must surely remain the constant occupation of every believer. In its fulfilment, the individual is directly responsible to Baha'u'llah. "Let him not wait for any directions," Shoghi Effendi urgently advises, "or expect any special encouragement, from the elected representatives of his community, nor be deterred by any obstacles which his relatives, or fellow-citizens may be inclined to place in his path, nor mind the censure of his critics or enemies."

order.why: This supplied passage from the Ridván 1989 message of the Universal House of Justice says that the primary response must be to teach, ourselves and others, at all levels of society and by all possible means, and asks the friends to be lighters of unlit candles. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Compare it with the readings on the lamp from which other lamps are lit. Why does it begin with teaching ourselves?

This supplied counsel, written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi in 1956, calls bringing the light of guidance to a new soul the greatest glory and honor, and bringing it to an entirely new area the most meritorious service, which is why the friends were encouraged to disperse to new territories. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Read it with the readings on travel. How does it relate the individual soul to the opening of new places?
shortened: The greatest glory and honor which can come to an individual is to bring the light of guidance to some new soul.

The most meritorious service which anyone could render is to bring the light of divine guidance and the quickening power of the spirit to an entirely new area. Humanity is crying for salvation; and it is only by the Baha'is going into the various areas of the world, that it can be brought to them. This is the reason the Guardian has encouraged all of the friends to disperse to new territories, for this is the hour for the quickening of the world.

order.why: This supplied counsel, written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi in 1957, calls the Bahá’ís the leaven of God which must leaven the lump of their nation, and says that the protection given to them and to their country is in direct ratio to their success, for unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. What does the image of leaven suggest about the size and influence of a community that teaches?

This supplied passage from the Ridván 1998 message of the Universal House of Justice says that the worldwide community’s unique success in representing the human race places it in a position of inescapable responsibility, a sacred duty toward everyone not yet aware of the call of God’s latest Manifestation, and asks, Dare we linger? No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Read it with the readings on the call. How does it turn achievement into obligation?
shortened: There is no other aggregation of human beings who can claim to have raised up a system with the demonstrated capacity to unite all of God's children in one world-embracing Order. This achievement places us not only in a position of incomparable strength, but more particularly in one of inescapable responsibility. Does not every one of us therefore have a divine obligation to fulfil, a sacred duty to perform towards every other one who is not yet aware of the call of God's latest Manifestation? Time does not stop, does not wait. With every passing hour a fresh affliction strikes at a distracted humanity. Dare we linger?

order.why: This supplied counsel, written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi in 1949, says that to find receptive souls and teach them, with tact and understanding, is the duty and privilege of every single Bahá’í. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Compare it with the readings on sowing in receptive soil. What is the difference between a duty and a privilege here, and why does it name both?

This supplied counsel, written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi in 1952, calls teaching the head corner-stone of all Bahá’í service, and says that successful teaching depends on many factors, among them the development of a true Bahá’í way of living and the fulfilment of the responsibilities we have incurred. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Read it with the readings on deeds and character. How does a way of living become a condition of teaching?

This supplied counsel, written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi in 1956, acknowledges that the friends often feel inadequate, tired and perhaps frightened before their tasks, calls this only natural, and says that the power of God can and will assist them, and that accepting the Manifestation has placed on them a great moral responsibility toward their fellow men. No catalogue record has been matched, so the wording remains as supplied with its unmatched status. Compare it with the readings on confirmations. How does it answer the feeling of inadequacy?

questions: The readings call teaching both the duty of every believer and the greatest gift of God. How do the sections on the call and on its reward fit together? Is a gift something one can be commanded to receive?

Bahá’u’lláh lifts the decree of the sword and ordains victory through utterance, yet many passages say deeds exert greater influence than words. How do utterance and deeds work together in the readings, and where would you place the warning that kindliness used only to convert is hypocrisy?

Several readings say to give the wine to the thirsty and otherwise keep it in its vessel, while others say to let no opportunity pass. How do the readings on receptive soil and on wisdom help a teacher hold these together?

The section on prudence records lands where teaching was forbidden or concealed. What do these passages show about wisdom, and how do they differ from the silence, fear and dread that ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says wisdom is not?

Many passages promise confirmation to those who arise, and others describe difficulty, slow response and weariness. Using the examples of Paul, the believer led with a halter, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s own journeys, consider what the readings say confirmation does and does not mean.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá puts promotion before organization, praises study classes and consultation, and asks each friend to befriend one soul a year. What would these counsels look like if a small group of friends in one neighborhood tried to follow them together?
